articles.title: In all-hands meeting, Jensen Huang thanks White House and says he’s in therapy
paragraphs: After a whirlwind period during which Jensen Huang’s life fell apart and then came back together again, the Nvidia founder now wants his staff to know that he’s a changed man.

Huang held Nvidia’s first all-hands meeting on Tuesday since his reinstatement on Monday. During that meeting, CNBC reported that Huang struck a “remorseful tone” and told the crowd “I hurt all of you.”

The founder, whose extramarital affairs have been accused of jeopardizing everything from the stock market to U.S. national security, went on to describe how difficult the current moment is for him: “This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang reportedly told staff.
“The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife,” he added.

The CEO admitted in the meeting that he had flouted Nvidia’s code of conduct, which he himself had largely devised. Huang emphasized that the code of conduct was still in effect, but that mitigating circumstances would matter a lot. As Wired reported Huang’s statement, it “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door.”
Huang told staff that he’s in therapy and also said that he was grateful for a second chance at the company.

The CEO is now walking a difficult tight rope between reasserting his authority over one of the world’s most powerful and influential companies, and conceding that he may have made some mistakes. He also tackled the difficult question of President Trump’s role in his restoration. The president reportedly called Nvidia’s board directly to lobby for Huang’s return, but in his talk, Huang downplayed Trump’s role

Huang thanked the administration on Tuesday for “providing Nvidia with quick access to intelligence that he said helped the board determine that the national security risks the company faced in reinstating him were low,” The Wall Street Journal writes.

articles.title: Even the best AI agents struggle with everyday life
paragraphs: AI companies have spent the last couple of months marketing personal AI agents as tools to take over the digital drudgery of human existence — and millions have been sold on the vision, handing over their shopping schedules, travel plans, and everyday responsibilities to AI assistants. But new research suggests that even the most advanced AI models struggle to reliably and safely navigate the messy details of people’s lives.

According to ShellBench, a new benchmark for everyday agent work, even the most advanced models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta failed more than a third of the time. Across all models tested, 15.7% of attempts failed at least one safety requirement, often leading to unintended consequences.

ShellBench was developed in collaboration with researchers at The OpenClaw Foundation, Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat, and UC Berkeley, drawing on more than 10 million anonymized, real-world AI agent interactions to see how agents perform on the everyday work people actually delegate to them.

The research comes as personal AI assistants are finding new popularity among developers, with Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic all fighting for a piece of the market with Muse, Dots, and Claude Duet, respectively.

In October, Meta said more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had set up its personal AI agent, Muse, within six weeks of launch, with about a quarter using it daily. That number is expected to grow as Meta implants Muse directly into Instagram DMs. Despite growing popularity among consumers, we still have little evidence about how reliable AI personal assistant products actually are.

ShellBench suggests that the unreliable nature of most everyday data sources still causes problems for many state-of-the-art systems. A successful agent should be able to navigate messy personal workspaces containing emails, calendar entries, spreadsheets, receipts, chat logs, outdated information, and phishing attempts, and figure out which information is relevant, what is private, and how to deliver the requested outcome without creating new problems.

It seems many of today’s AI agents are still not up to the task. Not only did even the highest-performing agents frequently fail to meet the requirements of a task, but they also lacked consistency. When researchers ran each task three times under identical conditions, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, the highest-scoring model, nailed all three attempts less than half the time.
For autonomous assistants that are meant to run in the background without supervision, it’s a problem if users need to run an agent multiple times to get a result they trust.

articles.title: Walmart teams up with Meta to bring Black Friday deals to AI agent Muse
paragraphs: Shopping with AI is becoming less of a futuristic idea and more of something companies expect us to do. Walmart is the latest retailer making that shift, teaming up with Meta to let customers shop its Black Friday deals through Muse, Meta’s AI agent.

The partnership, announced Tuesday, gives shoppers another way to find products, compare prices, and make purchases without browsing Walmart’s website themselves. Instead, customers can simply tell Muse what they are looking for and let the AI do the work.

The announcement highlights how differently Walmart and Amazon are approaching AI shopping. While Amazon has taken steps to stop third-party AI agents from making purchases for customers, Walmart is leaning into the idea.

To get started, users open the Muse app, sign in to their Walmart account, and return to the assistant to begin shopping. They can ask it to find specific products, compare options, or track down deals. Once a customer makes a request in Muse, the assistant sends it to Walmart, which returns relevant products and helps build a shopping cart.

Walmart says it has built privacy protections into the experience. For instance, Muse doesn’t get access to a customer’s Walmart shopping history or other personal information. Shoppers can also set spending limits, require approval before purchases, and review orders placed by the agent.
Plus, the company notes users can always delete their agent’s profile if they want to.

The experience is powered by Walmart’s Agent Gateway, a new system that allows outside AI assistants to connect directly with the retailer’s online store. This launched in October, and the company is planning to open it up to more developers and AI platforms, meaning Muse could eventually be just one of several assistants capable of shopping Walmart’s online store.
Walmart is not the only company teaming up with Meta’s Muse. Instacart also recently joined forces with the AI assistant.

articles.title: Maple raises $5.3M to build AI products that protect your data, even from itself
paragraphs: As AI assistants evolve into more capable agents that can access our files, emails, calendar, browser, and more, the amount of trust we’re expected to place in AI companies is growing. One startup called Maple, co-founded by a former Apple engineer who worked on privacy-preserving technologies, is taking a different approach with its AI app, where users’ data remains private — even from the company itself.

“We wanted to build something that was not only encrypted but also could be proven, and that people could go look at the open-source code, and then they could look at what we call trusted execution environments,” explains Maple co-founder and CEO Mark Suman. “They can look at and verify the code that’s running on our servers, so they don’t really have to take our word for it.”
“They can audit everything themselves and know how their data is being handled,” he adds.

The idea of trust is Maple’s larger theme, as the startup proposes that there’s a way to build an AI app where consumers don’t have to trade privacy for convenience, as its competitors often require with their invasive privacy policies, data collection practices, and sometimes even training on users’ personal data.
Instead of asking users to trust that Maple won’t misuse their personal data, it’s attempting to build a business where it can’t access that data in the first place.

Like other AI apps on the market, Maple allows users to engage in a chat experience where they ask questions and get answers. Meanwhile, its newly launched desktop app, Maple Work, offers a more agentic experience where the AI can control your computer, work with your files and apps, and control your browser to get online tasks handled.

With the company’s recently closed $5.3 million round, it’s moving on to its next product — a cloud-based agent that will be able to continue its work even if your computer isn’t on. This addition would make Maple more competitive with other popular consumer AI services, like Meta’s Muse, Instinct, and other AI agents that work over chat.
Suman, who previously spent six years at Apple, already had a background where AI and privacy overlapped, he tells TechCrunch.

articles.title: Anthropic shares fall below IPO price, a worrying sign for AI startups
paragraphs: Anthropic’s stock fell below its IPO price of $83, trading as low as $76 a share by midday Tuesday, down nearly 12% from Monday’s close.
Falling below the IPO price is often seen as a negative signal because underwriters typically price offerings at a discount to their expected trading value.

The AI industry has been eagerly watching how Anthropic’s shares trade, with VCs and other observers saying its performance could serve as a barometer for how public market investors value the sector.

The dramatic slump comes less than a week after Anthropic debuted on Nasdaq at $111.50 a share. If its shares continue to trade poorly in the coming weeks, the slide could put pressure on private startup valuations and weaken IPO prospects for other AI companies.

Anthropic isn’t the only AI stock selling off on Tuesday. Nvidia fell more than 7% by midday, giving back some of the more than 30%-plus gain it posted Monday after Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO.

articles.title: Raising the stakes for enterprise networks with AI modernization
paragraphs: Enterprise networks are under severe strain. As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on the network. Now, agentic AI is adding to the load. Tasks conducted by AI agents generate an estimated 450% more network traffic than the same tasks done by human workers.

As AI inference shifts from hyperscale training clouds—the huge centralized data centers where raw AI models ingest vast datasets and learn—to real-time, latency-sensitive applications, the need for on-premises or near-premises infrastructure grows. As a result, the gap between enterprise networks that are ready to support AI and those that are not is widening. As few as half of enterprises believe their current networks can handle AI’s bandwidth and latency demands, according to a recent study.
This report explores how treating network modernization as an on-going strategy rather than a one-off project can help organizations adapt in the face of disruption and uncertainty.

AI may force companies to shift from a cloud-first approach to routing workloads. Training AI requires server-to-server data center architectures, while inference calls for low-latency connectivity close to users. Enterprises may need to fundamentally reconsider their network architecture to meet these requirements.

AI inference is pushing infrastructure back on premises. Inference typically requires real-time processing and is sensitive to latency, making hosting such capabilities on distant hyperscale clouds neither economical nor practical. Inconsistent latency can lead to AI model failures, driving up queue wait times, saturating GPUs loads, and causing bottlenecks in data flows. Large enterprises may need on-premises or near-premises inference, which reverses years of cloud-first consolidation and forces new approaches to data center architecture, connectivity, and physical infrastructure.

AI workloads are stressing physical network capacity in unexpected ways. The traffic increase from agentic AI, combined with inference moving on-premises, is exposing bandwidth bottlenecks in legacy underlay infrastructure.

Network modernization is an ongoing project that requires a holistic approach, allowing companies to adapt with ease. A combination of strong architectural governance, reusable design templates, and retained internal expertise supports organizations in adapting to disruptive events without rebuilding their infrastructure from scratch each time. Such events could include mergers and acquisitions, changing vendors, or technology upgrades.

NaaS and AI-driven observability can improve efficiency and reduce complexity in network operations. Network-as-a-service (NaaS) and AI-driven observability can offer companies benefits like faster, more flexible provisioning and lower costs.

articles.title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
paragraphs: Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.

Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.

This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll, 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).

But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is, Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer.

You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea.
“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.

The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences.

articles.title: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
paragraphs: The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.

The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.

When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.
Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

articles.title: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
paragraphs: Nato chief Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz respond to reports of Russian plans to launch nuclear weapons into space
Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after reports that Russia was preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.

Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media outlets. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.
Asked about the reports, Rutte said: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hadn't seen the latest reports but dismissed reports citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".
The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".
Rutte told the press conference in Berlin that Nato had a variety of response options.
"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary," he said.

articles.title: What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
paragraphs: Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.

The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?
The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.
Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes, has called it "a dangerous escalation".
It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.
Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.

Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.

The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.

articles.title: Gisèle Pelicot 'humiliated' after nude photos sent to media to promote book
paragraphs: Gisèle Pelicot said she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay
Gisèle Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.
The 73-year-old told French broadcaster BFM TV she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay.

Pelicot made headlines across the world when she waived her right to anonymity in the trial of her then-husband Dominique, who was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious.
The publisher apologised, saying it would no longer print or promote the work after "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".
Pelicot told BFM: "I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes."
"Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt, as if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough," she said.
The essay was written by Sabine Prokhoris, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, who has previously criticised the Me Too movement.

articles.title: Democrats win House by largest margin in 50 years. And, COP31 ends with no deal
paragraphs: Your support helps make our show possible and unlocks access to our sponsor-free feed.

Vote counts are concluding for the 2026 midterm elections, revealing a better picture of just how much Democrats dominated. Fifty-six percent of voters chose the Democrats in House races compared to 42% for Republicans. The 14-point gap is the largest margin won by Democrats in 50 years. The party has officially won the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s. Take a look at NPR's breakdown of the U.S. House races, by the numbers.

Artificial intelligence is causing significant swings in the stock market as investors speculate about the future of the technology boom. While AI stocks have driven markets to record highs and bolstered the economy, concerns are growing about a potential bubble. Investors anticipated that AI giant Anthropic's stock market debut last week would lift markets, but instead Wall Street experienced one of its worst weeks in recent times.

Poland has called an emergency NATO session for today after Russia fired three cruise missiles into its territory. The incident highlights the stakes for European countries in Russia's war on Ukraine, prompting nations along NATO's eastern border to seek enhanced air defense support. Poland plans to present proposals to increase surveillance capabilities and deploy more F-35s to intercept incoming missiles and drones.

Delegates at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, couldn't agree on a plan over the weekend to address fossil fuels, the main cause of climate change. The event ran two days longer than expected, making it the longest in the history of these summits. Nearly 200 nations failed to finalize targets for electrification and financial aid for developing countries, or to address the impacts of climate change. The European Union rejected any conclusion that didn't advocate for a transition away from fossil fuels, while oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia opposed this position. Fossil fuels contribute about 73% of global emissions.

articles.title: Zelenskyy hails Ukraine's attack on a Russian warship docked at a naval base in Libya
paragraphs: In this image made from video provided by Russian Defense Ministry Press Service on Sunday, July 16, 2023, a Russian navy corvette Merkury attends naval military exercises in the Baltic Sea. Russian Defense Ministry Press Service/AP hide caption

KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine carried out an attack on a Russian warship moored at a port in Libya, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday, claiming that maritime drones sank the navy vessel in a surprise assault the previous day.

Ukrainian forces deployed seven drones in the operation that struck the Russian navy corvette in the Mediterranean, according to Zelenskyy. The ship, the Merkury, was one of Russia's newest vessels, commissioned a year after Moscow launched the 2022 full-scale invasion of its neighbor, he said in a post on X.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov declined to comment on the attack, saying that Russia's Defense Ministry would provide more information "if deemed to be appropriate."
The operation, conducted some 2,400 kilometers (1,500 miles) from the front line in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv's forces.

Ukraine has at times embarrassed Moscow during the war with attacks such as Operation Spiderweb in June 2025, when drones launched from trucks hit over 40 aircraft parked at air bases across Russia. Along the roughly 1,250-kilometer (almost 800-mile) front line snaking through eastern and southern Ukraine, Kyiv's drones and ground robots are helping hold back Russia's bigger army.
At the same time, Russia's missiles and drones have devastated Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter and damaged civilian buildings.

A Russian strike on a five-story apartment block in a village near Kyiv killed 11 people, regional police said Monday. A 7-year-old child and a 79-year-old woman were pulled alive from the rubble after the Sunday morning attack, rescue services said.

articles.title: Ukraine war spilling into NATO territory
paragraphs: The war between Russia and Ukraine once again creeps onto European territory – from attacks on ships to missiles in Poland and fresh allegations of Russian operations inside Denmark.

ROB SCHMITZ, HOST: A Russian ship was set ablaze after it was struck by a drone in the Baltic Sea. Yet another sign that the war in Ukraine is, at times, spilling over into the rest of Europe. This comes just days after President Trump called Russian President Vladimir Putin his friend. Teri Schultz joins us now from Brussels. Teri, let's start in the Gulf of Finland. A Russian cargo ship was hit by a drone there Saturday and caught fire. What's the latest on that?TERI SCHULTZ, BYLINE: Well, a few hours ago, Rob, Russia took control of this cargo ship, the Sparta II, and towed it out of Finnish waters a day after, as you mentioned, it was hit by a drone. The crew was rescued by another Russian vessel traveling nearby at the time of the strike. Now, the attack is presumed to have come from Ukraine, but Kyiv has not yet claimed responsibility. Finnish President Alexander Stubb referred to the incident as an unfortunate reminder that the, quote, "consequences of Russia's war of aggression are also visible in our region." Interestingly, teams from both Finland and neighboring Estonia came Saturday and helped Russian ships try to put out the fire on board. Stubb thanked all of those involved for what he called responsible and professional actions.SCHMITZ: So if the Sparta II was in the service of the Russian military, why didn't Finland seize the ship to put it out of business?SCHULTZ: There was a lot of talk about this in Finland because this ship transports weapons and other supplies to Russia to use against Ukraine. And the vessel itself is under U.S. and U.K. sanctions, and its owner is under European Union sanctions. But the conclusion this time was that it would create too big an environmental hazard to keep it in Finnish waters. Here's how it was described in a press conference by Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, the director of sea operations for the Finnish Border Guard.(SOUNDBITE OF PRESS CONFERENCE)JUKKA-PEKKA LUMILAHTI: (Through interpreter) If we would let the vessel burn, it would most likely sink. And after that, it would cause a major environmental risk for Finland and Estonia.SCHULTZ: So as much as Finland would be pleased to take a military cargo ship out of Moscow's arsenal, in this case, they were basically saying good riddance.SCHMITZ: So Ukraine is not the only one launching far-reaching strikes. Last Friday, Russia launched missiles into Polish territory. And I understand that you were there covering a nearby military exercise involving nearly a dozen countries, and it was that that was suspected to be Russia's reason for doing this, right?SCHULTZ: Yeah, that's right. There were three Russian cruise missiles that landed between 30 and 60 miles from this military exercise, which was training forces for what's envisioned to eventually be a peace-monitoring mission in post-war Ukraine. At the time, all we knew on the ground was that there were multiple air alerts, at one time even telling us to take cover. And that happens often in Poland, especially at that location just over a hundred miles from the Ukrainian border. But this is particularly risky for the Russians, as they never know whether they'll kill people from a NATO country on the ground. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte was asked by a crowd of reporters in Warsaw whether the alliance can do anything to stop these Russian incursions.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)MARK RUTTE: I cannot guarantee you that it will not happen. But I can guarantee you is that NATO will defend every inch of Polish territory, that as a collective alliance, we impose immense costs on Russians.SCHULTZ: Now, Rob, NATO ambassadors will meet Monday morning in a special session to discuss what more their countries may be able to do to protect Poland.SCHMITZ: That is Teri Schultz in Brussels. Teri, thanks so much for your reporting.SCHULTZ: You're welcome.

articles.title: Luxury development planned on land some Albanians say is theirs, not Jared Kushner's
paragraphs: A company working for President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner purchased 300 acres of Albanian land for more than $130 million in April. But Albanians in the area tell NPR this is not Kushner's land — it's theirs.

ROB SCHMITZ, HOST: In the summer of 2021, Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump boarded a yacht owned by Nat Rothschild, an heir to the European banking family. On the way from Montenegro to Greece, the yacht anchored off the coast of Albania, and as Kushner told an investment conference last year, that's when Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama arrived at the boat to tell them about his plan for the country.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)JARED KUSHNER: But I was very, very impressed with his vision for what he wanted to do with Albania. I really didn't know anything about the country. I didn't understand the history. And the darkness of the history with the communism and the terrible leadership actually led to it being fully undeveloped as a nation.SCHMITZ: A year later, Kushner was looking for development opportunities in the Balkans. He returned to the Albanian coast to the city of Vlorë, which was finishing the construction of an airport atop a wetland near an undeveloped coastline.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)KUSHNER: Obviously, a country is going to build an airport by the coast in the place that they think is the most beautiful. So we went there, we looked for opportunities, and we were able to find some incredible, incredible opportunities.SCHMITZ: And this is where Kushner found these opportunities.(SOUNDBITE OF WIND BLOWING)SCHMITZ: Hidrovor Beach is an expanse of caramel-colored sand with the gentle waves of the Adriatic lapping its perimeter. Albanian authorities say that a company working for Kushner purchased this land and hundreds of acres surrounding it for more than $130 million in April of this year. But several people in Albania tell NPR, this is not Kushner's land. They say it's theirs.GENTIAN MOÇKA: This land here belonged to my family for centuries.SCHMITZ: Gentian Moçka says his family has owned this strip of beach and wetlands since the time of the Ottoman Empire. He's provided NPR land titles that appear to prove this. After World War II, Albania's communist government seized it, along with all private land. When communism fell in 1991, families like Moçka's embarked on a yearslong process to get their land back.MOÇKA: But then our problems started with guys that were much more powerful than we were, had a lot of political support, were very rich and very well connected with the politics of that time.SCHMITZ: In 2006, Moçka learned that someone else was laying claim to his family's land, a man named Artur Shehu, who was a familiar name for those who lived here in the 1990s when the regional capital of Vlorë was outside the control of the country's government. It was instead run by Mafia-style gangs, as captured by news video from the AP at that time.(SOUNDBITE OF GUNFIRE)SCHMITZ: Artur Shehu was well known to police in Vlorë for his alleged involvement in a crime syndicate that, according to Albanian prosecutors, smuggled drugs and migrants into Europe. He fled Albania in 1999 after what police say was a shootout with a rival gang. He ended up in the United States, where he received asylum in 2001 and later became a U.S. citizen. The 60-year-old Shehu now lives in a villa in Miami Beach.But he's continued to manage a growing real estate portfolio back in Albania through an associate in Vlorë named Pëllumb Petritaj. The pair has claimed plots of land, including Moçka's family plot on the beach, up and down the southern Albanian coast, and prosecutors have taken notice. In 2018, Petritaj served three years in prison for forging land titles on behalf of Shehu. And on Wednesday, Petritaj was sentenced to another seven years in prison for falsifying documents to $17 million worth of oceanfront property in the city of Vlorë on behalf of Shehu. The court ordered the land confiscated from Shehu last week.(SOUNDBITE OF DOG BARKING)SCHMITZ: The pair has also claimed oceanfront farmland in the village of Zvërnec, adjacent to Moçka's beach.(SOUNDBITE OF DOG BARKING)SCHMITZ: The quiet village has only a couple hundred residents. Most of them, like Minela Konomi (ph) and Natasha Kota are past the age of 70. I asked them if they know who Artur Shehu is.MINELA KONOMI: (Non-English language spoken).SCHMITZ: "He is from the village of Kaninë, far from here up in the mountains," says Konomi, "but his family has never lived here. He's involved in shady dealings," Konomi says. Then Mrs. Kota speaks up.NATASHA KOTA: (Non-English language spoken).KOTA: "There wasn't a single soul of that family living here, going back to the Ottoman times," she says. "We've heard stories about him, and we're very scared of him."KOTA: (Non-English language spoken).SCHMITZ: Twenty years ago, Kota, Konomi and dozens of others in this village learned that Artur Shehu had somehow acquired their farmland. They filed suit in Albanian court to reclaim their land, a fight that escalated this past April when Shehu sold the parcel that includes what they say is their farmland to a company developing a luxury resort project for Kushner. That transaction, however, is under review. In court documents obtained by NPR, Albanian prosecutors argue that the land involved in Kushner's development is, quote, "suspected of having been illegally acquired through forgery."For his part, Kushner issued a statement on his website saying his partnership purchased the land from a private party in a private transaction. Title, he wrote, was reviewed by counsel and verified. NPR has reached out to Artur Shehu, but he did not respond. He has previously denied any wrongdoing.KUJTIM CAKRANI: (Non-English language spoken).SCHMITZ: However, a former lawyer for Shehu, a man named Kujtim Cakrani, was willing to talk.CAKRANI: (Non-English language spoken).SCHMITZ: Cakrani, dressed in a black suit and tie with slicked back hair, admits that individuals who were authorized by Artur Shehu as his power of attorney did forge documents related to the land that is now tied to Jared Kushner. He says Shehu's associates forged an inheritance certificate that made it appear that Shehu's grandfather had owned the land, which was then passed to Artur Shehu himself. And then last April, he sold that land to a pair of Syrian-born brothers who are now billionaires living in Qatar, Moataz and Ramez Al Khayyat. They are financial partners of Jared Kushner.CAKRANI: (Non-English language spoken).SCHMITZ: Cakrani says that when he discovered that Artur Shehu was involved in this forgery, he dropped him as his client. "It was too serious of a matter, and I can no longer defend him," Cakrani says. "And this is why," he says, "prosecutors have put Artur under investigation and have frozen his bank accounts." Cakrani says he is now representing a group of 30 relatives of Artur Shehu who he claims to be the rightful owners of this land.Thank you so much for your time.CAKRANI: Thank you.SCHMITZ: Gentian Moçka as well as Minela Konomi and Natasha Kota in Zvërnec tell NPR that nobody by the name of Shehu - Artur nor his relatives - has any legal claim to what they say is their land, oceanfront land that has now been claimed by several parties, including the son-in-law of the president of the United States.RODEN HOXHA: Now that it's Kushner in it, everybody is freaking out.SCHMITZ: Albanian real estate expert Roden Hoxha has seen this kind of land battle many times before. He says land ownership in Albania is complicated by decades under a Stalinist regime that stole all the land from private owners and collectivized it. And when communism fell in 1991, he says Albania became a land-grab free-for-all.HOXHA: And it was so disorganized - it was basically chaos - that people started claiming land wherever, you know, they threw a stone. It was basically the Albanian version of U.S.'s claiming of the West.SCHMITZ: Complete, Hoxha says, with wealthy speculators, keen to exploit the chaos of the moment and with multiple levels - locals whose families have farmed the land for generations, well-connected operators like Shehu who aggressively try to claim that land.HOXHA: And then on the international level, it exploded because it was Kushner and Trump and Arab money behind it.SCHMITZ: And Hoxha says, what at first appeared to be yet another Albanian land dispute now has ties all the way to the White House. In the end, an Albanian court will likely decide who the rightful owner of this property is. But for now, the corruption this deal suggests has sparked unprecedented public outrage in Albania.(SOUNDBITE OF EXPLOSIONS)SCHMITZ: Protesters have taken to the streets of the capital, Tirana, every day since May 31, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign, but Rama has only vowed to crack down harder on what have become increasingly violent demonstrations against his entire government. Rama has vowed that Kushner's resort project will go ahead as planned, but an ongoing investigation by Albania's state prosecutor into forged land titles could halt the project.(CHEERING)SCHMITZ: When contacted by NPR, a spokesperson for Prime Minister Edi Rama sent a statement which read that, quote, "if the seller does not have legitimate ownership of the property, the money will remain within the Republic of Albania. And certainly, it will be used for anyone who proves that his claim over the property is grounded." The statement went on to say that the ambition for Rama's government is to create a new benchmark for sustainable Mediterranean development, a goal that aligns with Jared Kushner's vision for a luxury resort, a five-star ecotourism site, as his wife, Ivanka Trump laid out in a podcast episode called "Ivanka Trump On Building The Authentic Life."(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)IVANKA TRUMP: For me, it feels more like a challenge than anything else, the culmination of all of my experience in real estate, all of my travel, a lot of reflection on how I want to live.SCHMITZ: In the podcast, Trump described both the Zvërnec beachfront property, as well as an island across from it, named Sazan, as part of a development project belonging to her and Kushner.(SOUNDBITE OF BOAT MOTOR RUNNING)SCHMITZ: Getting to Sazan from the mainland takes about an hour by boat. Today, tour operator Sharif Durmichai (ph), who insists I call him by his nickname Capitan Bacchi (ph), takes me to the uninhabited island.SHARIF DURMICHAI: (Non-English language spoken).SCHMITZ: When we get there, we hike up a trail past foxholes. Signs along the trail warn passersby to stick to the trail lest they step on a landmine. For years, this island was a fortified military outpost. I ask him what he thinks about Trump and Kushner's plans for the region and the protests that have followed them.DURMICHAI: (Non-English language spoken).SCHMITZ: "I work in tourism," he says, "and I'm from here. If you've seen how local developers, along with the local Mafia, have built this region, it's a massacre," he says. "They've destroyed so much of what is a beautiful coastline. I support the Kushner project because it's going to be ecologically sustainable, and it will set a good benchmark for future projects. We are a small country," Capitan Bacchi says, "and Kushner and Trump are very big names." Big names that'll be in the crosshairs of an incoming Democratic Congress back in the U.S.JAMIE RASKIN: This is an individual in the Trump family who has essentially been two-timing on the American people.SCHMITZ: Democratic Maryland Congressman Jamie Raskin will soon head the House Judiciary Committee and will have power to investigate and subpoena members of the president's family. He says he'll be focusing on Jared Kushner, who he says has been splitting his time between foreign policy and making business deals on the side.RASKIN: American foreign policy has never seen anything like that before. And in this, of course, he is only imitating his father-in-law, who declared that he got $2.2 billion on the side in his first year in office. That's more than $1 million an hour.SCHMITZ: Congressman Raskin says the luxury resort project in Albania is one of many Kushner-backed deals that have prompted investigative inquiries from his committee, and there could be more as the new Congress is sworn in.

articles.title: Lebanese villagers return to wrecked homes as the Israeli army pulls back
paragraphs: A destroyed home in the village of Zawtar al-Gharbiyah in southern Lebanon. The family says Israeli forces demolished their home and two other homes of extended family when they occupied the village after a U.S.-brokered ceasefire. Mohammad Yassine for NPR hide caption

ZAWTAR AL-GHARBIYAH, Lebanon — After two decades of working installing vehicle air conditioning in Saudi Arabia, Atef Kadouh saved up enough money to build a house in his hometown in southern Lebanon.
He and his wife, Soumaya Yaghi lived in the house for 40 years and had five children — all born at home.
A photo of the youngest, Adel, is propped up in a basket of dried flowers near the doorway.

Adel, clean-cut with a trimmed beard, was a sports teacher and a basketball champion who was planning to travel to France this summer to pursue his doctorate. When the war with Israel began this year, he decided to volunteer as an ambulance driver.

Soumaya Yaghi stands in her damaged home. Israeli forces occupied the house while they were in the village and it was set on fire as they left. The second floor was burned almost completely. Mohammad Yassine for NPR hide caption
The Israeli military killed him and four other medics on March 28 in a drone strike as the first responders buried a 75-year-old man who had died in hospital.

"This one broke me," his father says. "He was my youngest son, 27 years old. There have been wars in every country in the world but there are rules for war … you attack a paramedic rescuing wounded people, children? He was not a fighter at the front."

articles.title: US rapper postpones two arena shows after Manchester evacuation
paragraphs: US rapper Don Toliver has postponed two shows in London this week, after his concert in Manchester on Sunday was evacuated when an "unknown substance" was released into the crowd.
Toliver was due to play The O2 on Monday and Wembley Arena on Tuesday, but Live Nation said his "stage and production equipment remains in Manchester and cannot be moved in time".
One person was taken to hospital and 89 people showed "symptoms believed to be linked to the exposure" after Sunday's Co-op Live arena show, police said.
Fans described "distressing scenes" with people "choking", "screaming" and "coughing up blood" because of the effects of a substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas.
Watch: Coughs, confusion and boos as Co-op Live concert cancelled
The Wembley show has been rescheduled to 14 December, while Monday night's O2 gig has been moved to 15 December.
"I'm very sad to sit here and say I have to reschedule The O2 London show to December 15th due to (the) unfortunate incident last night," Don Toliver wrote on Instagram.
Greater Manchester Police (GMP) declared a major incident on Sunday and said 12,000 people were evacuated from the arena.

articles.title: Police investigate unknown substance that caused Manchester's Co-op Live evacuation
paragraphs: Watch: Coughing, confusion and boos as Co-op Live concert cancelled
Police are investigating after thousands of people were evacuated from a concert in Manchester following an "unknown substance" being released into the crowd.

It happened towards the end of US rapper Don Toliver's show at the Co-op Live arena at about 22:00 GMT on Sunday, with fans describing a "horrible smell" and people "screaming" and "coughing up blood".
One woman was taken to hospital for treatment, while 88 other people were assessed by paramedics for "eye and respiratory symptoms".
Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said detectives were trying to establish what the substance was and where it came from and further testing was taking place on items found at the venue.
A major incident was declared after reports of people suffering from the effects of an unknown substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas.
That major incident status was lifted at about 04:00 GMT.
The force said no arrests had yet been made and detectives were investigating "whether any criminality has occurred in relation to this incident".

articles.title: Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in California ceremony
paragraphs: Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California.
A string of black and white photos shared by the Flowers singer on Instagram showed the pair kissing while surrounded by white roses.

Her mother, Trisha Cyrus, and sister, Noah Cyrus, could be seen in the background of one image. Her father Billy Ray Cyrus was not in the picture but was at the ceremony with his partner, actress Liz Hurley.
Grammy-winning Cyrus, 33, wore a white silk dress designed by Anthony Vaccarello for Saint Laurent, while 28-year-old drummer Morando said "I do" in a black suit from the same fashion house.
In one of the photographs, which was the first in a series of images shared by the singer in an Instagram post, the newly weds posed next to a golden retriever.
The post was captioned with "M+M" followed by a white heart and the ceremony date, 21 November.
Miley's sister Brandi Cyrus, singer Doechii and fashion designer Donatella Versace were among those to congratulate the couple in the comments.
The ceremony reportedly took place at a resort formerly owned by Fly Me To The Moon singer Frank Sinatra.

articles.title: Britain's Got Talent winner almost missed audition due to Carphone Warehouse shift
paragraphs: Paul Potts was managing Port Talbot's Carphone Warehouse store at the time of his audition
Britain's Got Talent winner Paul Potts said he nearly missed his life-changing audition on the show because he had been unable to get time off from his job managing a phone shop.

The tenor shot to fame in 2007 after performing Nessun Dorma on the ITV talent show, but had unsuccessfully tried to change the date of his performance because of his shift at Port Talbot's Carphone Warehouse.
"It was only thanks to a colleague who normally didn't work Saturdays that came into cover me – otherwise I wouldn't have been there," he said.
He has since released six albums, reached the final of America's Got Talent: The Champions and inspired the Hollywood film One Chance.
"I actually almost didn't end up going," he told BBC Radio Wales' My Welsh Life.
Almost 20 years later, as he prepares for a special homecoming concert in Port Talbot, Potts said he was honoured to be "still doing what I love doing".
"The only reason why I'm still doing that is because people still support me and I'll always be forever grateful for that."

articles.title: Berlinale Alum Sreemoyee Singh’s WAVES Film Bazaar Selection ‘Fireflowers,’ About a Mother’s Lost Singing Voice, Boards Dutch Co-Producer (EXCLUSIVE)
paragraphs: Indian filmmaker Sreemoyee Singh’s personal documentary “Fireflowers,” about a mother who lost her singing voice after her husband died, has added Dutch outfit New Amsterdam Film Company, through Sander Verdonk, as co-producer.
The project is also among the selections at this year’s WAVES Film Bazaar, the market component of the International Film Festival of India in Goa.

The co-production was finalized ahead of the market. “Fireflowers” is Singh’s follow-up to “And, Towards Happy Alleys,” her debut documentary, which she shot in Iran and which world premiered in the Berlinale’s Panorama strand in 2023. Related Stories Paul W. Downs, Jen Statsky and Lucia Aniello to Earn Commitment to California Award at Hollywood Chamber of Commerce’s 2026 Entertainment Industry Conference Tyson Fury Reveals Schizophrenia Diagnosis in Netflix Documentary: ‘I Thought I’d End Up in a Padded Room’

The new film turns to Singh’s own family. Her parents used to sing together, and within a year of her father’s death, her mother could no longer sing. Singh began training in vocal music around the same time. The film moves between her father’s 1980s Calcutta and the present day, as mother and daughter work through grief that was never fully dealt with, in a city that is itself losing much of its old character. Animation is by Bob and Bobby.

“This is a story I have been born into, lived and grown with. Finally I feel ready to share it. I filmed my debut documentary in Iran, but here I turn the lens inward – into my home, and tell the story of my parents and the city I have grown up in,” says Singh.

“In ‘Fireflowers,’ Sreemoyee Singh brings together her mother’s lost voice, her father’s absence and a disappearing Calcutta [Kolkata] in one intimate film. After her acclaimed Berlinale debut, I’m thrilled to support her as co-producer on this deeply personal and universal story,” says Verdonk.

Triparna Banerjee and Singh produce for Happy Alley Films, with Dibya Chatterjee and Indraprasad Ghatak of HandyKraft Pictures also co-producing. The project was earlier pitched at DocEdge Kolkata and has received support from South Korea’s DMZ Docs.

“‘Fireflowers’ is a mother and a daughter reflecting on grief, memory and the fragility of voice, held together by music and the city of Calcutta [Kolkata]. Producing it is my quiet resistance to the expectation that documentaries from India or South Asia must be boxed into social issues,” says Banerjee.

articles.title: Anya Taylor-Joy ‘Went Mute’ on ‘Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum’ Set When Ian McKellen Showed Up: ‘That’s F—ing Gandalf’
paragraphs: Anya Taylor-Joy, who is set to play Seren, an elf, in “The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum,” says the last time she found herself starstruck was when she first came face-to-face with Ian McKellen as Gandalf on set.
“I wasn’t prepared,” she told Dazed. “I went mute. And he’s the loveliest, funniest, most wonderful man and actor. But that’s fucking Gandalf!”

While Taylor-Joy didn’t let much else slip about the highly anticipated film in her cover story, she told the outlet she had specifically hoped to land a role in a “Lord of the Rings” film. “I had called my agent earlier on ‘Dune,’ being like, ‘If they ever make ‘The Lord of the Rings,’ let them know that I’d be interested,’” she said. Related Stories Byron Allen's BuzzFeed Hires Chris Poydenis, Co-Founder of Creator Marketing Agency Influential, as Chief Revenue Officer 'Daredevil' Star Charlie Cox Asked to Audition for James Bond but Was Told He's Too Old: 'Robert Pattinson Is the Same Age as Me!'

While McKellen originated the role of Gandalf in Peter Jackson’s “The Lord of the Rings” trilogy, a number of newcomers will make their franchise debut with “The Hunt for Gollum,” including Kate Winslet as Marigol and Leo Woodall as Halvard. Mainstays including Elijah Wood (Frodo) and Lee Pace (King Thranduil) are also set to reprise their roles. Andy Serkis pulls double duty, playing Gollum while also directing the film, while Jamie Dornan replaces Viggo Mortensen as Aragorn.

Back in July, Taylor-Joy admitted to Variety she hadn’t yet read the “Lord of the Rings” books despite landing the role in the forthcoming film. “I’m about to read the books now, actually,” she told Variety’s Marc Malkin. “So as a child, I had a misguided idea that you could only be a ‘Harry Potter’ fan or a ‘Lord of the Rings’ fan. Nobody told me that. I just came up with that on my own. Luckily, throughout COVID, I then watched all of ‘Lord of the Rings,’ and turns out you can love both, and you should.”

Malkin also asked the actress about her reaction to getting cast in “The Hunt for Gollum” at the time, to which she responded: “It’s so fun. I mean, if my tombstone can say ‘Lethal Elf,’ I feel like I did a good job on this planet. So yeah, I’m excited.” Dornan, her co-star, recently admitted he “cried” when he heard he’d gotten the job.

Nearly a year before “Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum” opens in theaters next Dec., Taylor-Joy will return to the big screen in Denis Villeneuve’s final “Dune” film, due out Dec. 18. In the film, she returns to play Alia Atreides, the younger sister of Paul.

articles.title: Woody Harrelson Turned Down Haymitch Offer Twice: I Didn’t ‘Think There Was Enough to Do’ in ‘The Hunger Games’
paragraphs: While a certain generation might associate Woody Harrelson most with his role as Haymitch Abernathy in the billion-dollar “Hunger Games” franchise, the actor has admitted he needed convincing to sign on for the dystopian film.

During a recent Vanity Fair interview alongside his “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” co-star Joseph Zada (who plays a younger Abernathy in the prequel), Woody told the actor he “turned it down twice,” referring to the role. Related Stories Trump Posts Bizarre AI Meme of Jensen Huang Holding Up a Bra, Riffing Off 2024 Assassination Attempt on President, After Nvidia Board Reinstates CEO Steven Spielberg to Direct Western Movie Starring Cillian Murphy, Jessie Buckley; Paul Thomas Anderson to Write Script Based on ‘The Heart in Winter’

“Turned it down?” asked Zada. “Yeah, it’s stupid,” responded Harrelson. “I thought it was good, I read the books, really good, but I just don’t think there’s enough to do. I don’t know if there’s enough to do. It’s an arbitrary, odd way of assessing it.”

He continued, explaining that director Gary Ross ultimately convinced him to do it. “[I] Can’t imagine not having had this experience in my life and knowing these people and then Gary calls me and he’s like, ‘Woody, you have to do this part. I don’t have a second choice. You have to play Haymitch.’ And he just talked to me for about 10 minutes on the phone. I’m like, ‘All right, okay, yeah, let’s do it.'”

Released in 2012, Ross directed the first “Hunger Games” film, while Francis Lawrence went on to direct “Catching Fire,” “Mockingjay – Part 1,” “Mockingjay – Part 2,” “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes” and “Sunrise on the Reaping.” The recently released prequel takes place 25 years before the original “Hunger Games” series and follows the origin story of Abernathy as he’s forced to compete in the second Quarter Quell. McKenna Grace, Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Elle Fanning and more also star.

In addition to Harrelson, who returned for the film, original cast members Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson also made small appearances. On an episode of “Call Her Daddy,” Lawrence told host Alex Cooper it was “unbelievable” to return as Katniss. “It was so crazy. It was the same crew. It was the same AD, who I’ve worked with a million times because I love him. And with Josh [Hutcherson] and Woody [Harrelson] … it was so emotional.”
“Sunrise on the Reaping” opened to $120 million at the box office last weekend, and is currently in theaters.

articles.title: Marathi Crime Drama ‘Hurda – That Tight Green Top’ Puts a Journalist’s Masculinity Under the Microscope at WAVES Film Bazaar
paragraphs: Apurv Gaikwad is presnting his debut feature “Hurda – That Tight Green Top,” a Marathi-language crime drama adapted from Atharva Pandit’s novel, to the Co-Production Market at WAVES Film Bazaar.

The film follows Chitranshu, a journalist investigating the mysterious deaths of three young sisters in a village in Maharashtra. When he returns to the village six years later, his search for the truth takes an unexpected turn, forcing him to confront uncomfortable realities.

Gaikwad says he was drawn to the story because he “was fascinated by its polyphonic narrative, the way multiple characters coexist, each with their own distinct voice.” He adds, “Even months after reading the novel, there was one particular aspect of it that refused to leave me – the protagonist, Chitranshu.”

“It is as much a mystery as it is a character study and an exploration of the society we live in. While the audience may find the answers they initially seek, I hope they leave the film with an entirely different set of questions,” says Gaikwad, who previously made the short mockumentary “The Last Auteur.”

Gaikwad hopes to challenge the binary understanding of masculinity and “the comfortable distinction we make between good men and bad men. I hope the film encourages audiences to question their own prejudices and examine how caste, gender and social hierarchies shape their understanding of truth, justice and morality,” he says.

The film is being produced by brothers Apurv and Akshay Gaikwad and Nina Bhatt of Disha Cinema and Khan & Kumar Media (“Songs of Forgotten Trees”). In an advanced stage of pre-production, the film is scheduled to start shooting in January 2027. Akassh Ghosalkar leads the cast, which also includes Rohit Kokate, Jitendra Lad, Gayatri Bansode and Gauri Deshpande.

Producer Nina Bhatt says she was drawn to Gaikwad’s examination of ordinary masculinity. “The contradictions between how men see themselves and how they exercise power in everyday relationships, his exploration of the entitlement and complicity that can exist within familiarity, affection and even empathy, felt particularly compelling to me. What made me want to back the project was his willingness to turn that examination inwards, rather than simply locate violence in others.”

Producer Vikas Kumar says Khan & Kumar believes in nurturing and supporting new and important voices in cinema, and that he strongly believes Gaikwad is one of them. “Supporting ‘Hurda’ felt like a natural progression of that belief.”

articles.title: Bela Bajaria Reflects on Her Netflix Experience and Says ‘Stay Tuned’ at International Emmy Awards
paragraphs: France takes drama series win for period piece 'Carême'; Argentina nabs comedy for 'División Palermo'; Turkey's 'Leyla' recognized for telenovela

Former Netflix executive Bela Bajaria put the emphasis on her belief in the transformative power of storytelling while accepting the Founders Award Monday night at the International Emmy Awards in New York.

Bajaria was ousted from her role as chief content officer of Netflix in a very public fashion last month amid a larger shake-up of content leadership at the streaming giant. In her speech — her first major public appearance since her departure — Bajaria reflected on her career journey to the top echelon of Hollywood as a senior executive at CBS and Universal Television before joining Netflix in 2016.

In a nod to this week’s Thanksgiving holiday, Bajaria opened by expressing her gratitude for the opportunities she’s been afforded since her family relocated to Southern California in the late 1970s, when she was in grade school.

“Gratitude isn’t passive or soft. It’s earned. Gratitude is strength in knowing nothing is guaranteed, and nothing can be taken for granted. Gratitude is the appreciation for both struggle and success, and sharing the journey with others,” Bajaria told the crowd.

During most of the past decade, Bajaria was focused on building out Netflix’s local-language TV content operation at a scale never before seen in the industry. The experience was profound as the regional teams set off on a search for new creative voices.

“Whether I was in Mumbai or Madrid, Bangkok or Berlin or anywhere in between — there’s nothing like being on the ground finding that original voice — in their homes, or sharing a meal, and looking eye to eye with openness, curiosity and respect,” Bajaria said. “I’ve seen firsthand how the saying is true: to paraphrase, you can ‘travel the world and never be a stranger.’ ”
Bajaria indicated pride in the legacy of her role having greatly expanded the global village of television during her tenure at Netflix.

articles.title: Shanghai Golden Goblet Winner Ridham Janve Stages a Goan Village Death Watch in ‘Goodbye Mr D’Mello’ at WAVES Film Bazaar
paragraphs: Ridham Janve, whose “Hunter’s Moon” won the Golden Goblet Award for best screenplay at the Shanghai International Film Festival this year, is bringing “Goodbye Mr D’Mello,” a dark comedy set in a Goan village, to the Co-Production Market at WAVES Film Bazaar.

The film centers on an elderly professor who announces on his village WhatsApp group that he knows exactly when he is going to die, setting off a series of absurd reactions within the community. Through a colorful ensemble of characters, the film explores human curiosity, superstition, gossip, greed, faith and our uneasy relationship with mortality. Related Stories Marvel’s ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Won’t Screen for BAFTA, Golden Globes and Other Early Awards Groups to Guard Its Spoilers (EXCLUSIVE) Trump Posts Bizarre AI Meme of Jensen Huang Holding Up a Bra, Riffing Off 2024 Assassination Attempt on President, After Nvidia Board Reinstates CEO

“Living in Goa, I have been fascinated by the peculiarities of its social life, its people, humor and contradictions,” says Janve, who developed the screenplay with Goan journalist and writer Mayabhushan Nagvenkar. “There is also something fascinating about how traditional village gossip has found new life through WhatsApp and social media. It is also both amusing and disturbing about how easily another person’s private life can become a public spectacle.”
Janve’s debut feature, “The Gold-Laden Sheep and the Sacred Mountain,” premiered at the International Film Festival Rotterdam (IFFR). His second, “Hunter’s Moon,” premiered in Shanghai.

The film is being produced by Sharib Khan and Vikas Kumar through Khan & Kumar Media, alongside Nagvenkar through Mountain Motion Pictures, Janve’s production company. This is the producers’ second collaboration with Janve, following “Hunter’s Moon.”

Kumar says, “We admire the passion and honesty of Ridham’s filmmaking. His first two features grew from years of close engagement with the Gaddi community in the Himalayas, and we have witnessed first-hand the care he takes to create worlds that feel genuinely lived-in. ‘Goodbye Mr D’Mello’ is very different in tone, but equally personal.”

Khan & Kumar Media’s recent productions include “Sonsi” (“Shadow Bird”); “Songs of Forgotten Trees” (winner of the Horizons best director award, Venice Film Festival 2025); “Lovers in the Blue Night” (Venice Film Festival, Horizons section, Netpac award winner, 2026); and “The Ink-Stained Hand and the Missing Thumb” (Karlovy Vary International Film Festival, 2026).

The producers plan to fund the film through co-producers, private financiers and institutional support. “Our production approach is lean and financially disciplined, drawing on existing locations, local resources and talent in Goa while maintaining the film’s creative ambitions,” says Kumar.

articles.title: Tarkowski's first Premier League red ruins Moyes' night - was it deserved?
paragraphs: It had been some run for Everton captain James Tarkowski.
Prior to Monday night, the defender had received 74 yellow cards in the Premier League but had never been sent off - a top-flight record.
But that run came to an end at Brentford as he was given his first red card in his 351st Premier League appearance, although the decision has attracted plenty of debate.

His dismissal crucially means he will miss Sunday's Merseyside derby and also ruined David Moyes' record-breaking night as he took charge of his 593rd game as Everton boss - more than anyone else in the club's history.
The 4-0 loss was also the heaviest defeat Everton have had since Moyes returned to the club at the start of last year.
Tarkowski's dismissal proved a big talking point during and after the match, with opinions split on whether he should have gone. Even Moyes wasn't sure.

He told BBC Match of the Day: "My thoughts at the time, I didn't think it was but when I've looked at it again I think his foot high. Is there enough force for it to be a red card? Not sure about that."
James Tarkowski received his first Premier League red card

articles.title: 'No-one's coming to save us' - but how can Man Utd save themselves?
paragraphs: Manchester United lost 4-0 at Liverpool in their opening match under Mauricio Pochettino
Manchester United's Premier League trip to Anfield was described by some as a free hit for new head coach Mauricio Pochettino.
The theory was expectations for United were so low as they travelled to Liverpool that a positive outcome would be a huge bonus, and anything else was expected.
But Pochettino did not look like a man without pressure after 15 minutes of what turned into a 4-0 defeat.

By that point, his side were already 2-0 behind and down to 10 men. Liverpool's fans were gleefully singing about the Argentine being "sacked in the morning", even though he was only a sixth of the way through his first game in charge.
A day later, United supporters began filtering through Manchester Airport on their way to Lisbon for a Champions League match that marks the next stop in what has turned into a desperate campaign.
The prevailing mood was one of resigned acceptance punctuated by dark humour around what a season in the Championship might look like, and whether Manchester City might be there with them.
United's England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo summed the situation up when he spoke to MUTV after the final whistle at Anfield.

articles.title: Who has made Troy's Premier League team of the week?
paragraphs: After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week.
Here are this week's choices. Do you agree? Give us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page.

Konstantinos Tzolakis (Hull City): If you watched the Brighton game and wondered how on earth Hull won it was because Konstantinos Tzolakis was in goal. An unbelievable performance with five or six top-class saves. Big moments, big personality, he has stepped up every time. He's been one of the players of the season - I know it's a bit too early to crown people but if it stopped now he has to be goalkeeper of the season.
Janelt scores stunner and Lewis-Potter nets twice as Brentford beat 10-man Everton

James Hill (Bournemouth): He backed up getting into the England squad. Sometimes when people get called up they start to get above their stations but he didn't do that at all. He was in a really good state of form. A cheeky assist as well but defensively solid. He has been in my team a few times now - a centre-half who does his job without complaining.
Malick Thiaw (Newcastle): He divides opinion but he played really well and got his goal.
Keane Lewis-Potter (Brentford): Two goals against Everton and that was before the sending-off of James Tarkowski. Performed well again. Sneaky bargain buy of the century to be honest.

Noah Okafor (Leeds): Two goals again. Leeds battered Chelsea and made them look unbelievably average. Nobody has been talking about how sneaky good Leeds have been, some really big performances this season.

articles.title: De Bruyne's feelings for Man City will 'never change'
paragraphs: Kevin de Bruyne won six Premier League titles, the Champions League, two FA Cups and five League Cups during his time at Manchester City
Kevin de Bruyne says his feelings for Manchester City will "never change" even if the club are stripped of their titles after being found guilty of breaching the Premier League's financial rules.
De Bruyne, 35, enjoyed a trophy-laden decade at Etihad Stadium, lifting 16 trophies including the Treble in 2023 before leaving on a free transfer to join Napoli in 2025.
The Belgian returns to City for the second time on Tuesday when Napoli play them in the Champions League.
De Bruyne says he has "nothing but affection" for the club and that "will never change" even if City were forced to give up their domestic titles.
"Of course, it's a lot of things that's been going on but I cannot change anything about that. I am proud of what I have done as a football player and, honestly, this is my club," he said.
"I love the owners, I have talked about a lot of stuff outside football - I have even spoken to [chairman] Khaldoon [Al Mubarak] about how to buy a club."
City deny any wrongdoing and are appealing the decision.

articles.title: England's tearaway quick bowler reinvented as a top-order batter
paragraphs: Sportspeople are faced with a question when injuries hit again and again. Do I try one more time or should I walk away?
England's Katie George came really close to choosing the latter option last year.
"I had a couple of conversations with my close family and partner about whether it was taking too much out of me and whether I was happy with the person I was," she says. "I was pretty miserable."
George made her England debut in 2018 aged 18 as a tearaway fast bowler. She was quick. Some coaches believed generationally so.

She played seven internationals between March and July before the injuries first hit that summer. George is matter of fact about how many have followed. The list is enough to make the rest of us wince.
"Nine stress fractures in my back," she says. "I tore the cartilage off my rib.
"Bits and bobs. Ankle surgery. I have missed a lot of cricket."

Unable to bowl because of her back and little more than a tailender with the bat, George got into sides purely for her athleticism and a penchant for stunning catches. She was occasionally referred to as a 'specialist fielder'.

articles.title: Lewis-Potter double and Janelt stunner ease Brentford past 10-man Everton
paragraphs: It was a record-breaking occasion in more ways than one. David Moyes made history for Everton, edging clear of Harry Catterick by overseeing his 593rd game in charge of the club, but calamitous defending ruined the Scot’s evening and defeat to Brentford was inevitable after James Tarkowski received his first red card in 351 Premier League appearances.

Those in Tarkowski’s corner will claim the Everton captain’s tackle on Yehor Yarmoliuk would not have been a foul back in the day. This, though, was not a “game’s gone” moment. Not that sort of player? The reality is Tarkowski’s back catalogue features plenty of orange card tackles, meaning there was always likely to come a time when his luck ran out.

Everton, whose passive performance denied them the chance to go fifth, should not bother complaining about Matthew Donohue’s intervention from Stockley Park after Tarkowski went in on Yarmoliuk with his studs raised late in the first half. It was the defender’s first red since he was playing for Brentford in the Championship and it had no great bearing on the result. Brentford led 2-0 before their former player went off, Keane Lewis-Potter’s third and fourth goals of the season putting them in control, and dominated from start to finish.

Keith Andrews, a young coach who will have done something right if he comes close to matching Moyes’s longevity, revelled in his side moving sixth thanks to an outstanding display. Moyes has been around long enough to know the top flight has rarely been this open but on this evidence Brentford look likelier than Everton to upset the established order.
It was a drubbing, a cracking third from Vitaly Janelt followed by Fábio Carvalho making it 4-0 in added time, and made clear that Brentford have the tools to challenge for European qualification.

With Igor Thiago unavailable after his controversial red card against Brighton it fell to Callum Wilson to lead the line for Brentford. Everton were unsettled by Wilson’s movement and were strangely muted. They sat in a low block but were not compact, were careless in possession and did not deal with Brentford’s wing play and midfield interchanges.

Jaidon Anthony, Mikkel Damsgaard and Michael Kayode had chances before Everton cracked. They were caught out by a long ball down the left and were undone when a poor clearing header led to a moment of brilliance from Anthony, the winger’s cushioned touch with the outside of his right foot running for Lewis-Potter to beat Jordan Pickford thanks to a deflection off Jarrad Branthwaite.

Brentford love to make the most of Lewis-Potter’s attacking instincts after converting him into a left-back. He joined as a winger and his runs are always a threat but Everton did not pay close enough attention. They were abysmal in the first half and faced more pressure when Vitaliy Mykolenko conceded a free-kick after losing Dango Ouattara. Damsgaard crossed, Everton were all at sea and Lewis-Potter scored via another deflection, this time off Thierno Barry.

articles.title: The 2035 Women’s World Cup has huge potential for women and girls in UK
paragraphs: Maximising the societal impact of the tournament, especially combating misogyny, should be a top priority
The announcement that the 2035 Women’s World Cup will be hosted in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland has finally come and, if we aim high enough, it could have a massive societal impact.
Confirmation was a foregone conclusion – the UK was the only bidder – but that did not mean the submission was complacent or lacked ambition.
This tournament, which will be the largest single-sport event staged in the UK, has the potential to transform women’s football in the four host nations and leave a positive wider imprint.

Andy Burnham said as much in his statement after the announcement, saying it “will reach into communities across the country, bring more people into the game and leave a legacy that lasts long after the final whistle”.
In a world where the manosphere is having an increasingly negative and misogynistic influence on young boys and men, the potential impact of a Women’s World Cup on home soil cannot be underestimated.

It is a large-scale problem. A Guardian article in March highlighted that almost a third of Gen Z men and boys think a wife should obey her husband. A 2025 Movember report found that 63% of young men watch masculinity influencers. In September 2023, a YouGov report found that one in six boys aged six to 15 had a positive opinion of Andrew Tate.
The task for the next eight and a half years, and beyond the tournament, is to ensure the 2035 Women’s World Cup isn’t just a great elite football event but that its impact far beyond is maximised.

articles.title: Nations Championship finals weekend to kick off in front of 40,000 empty seats
paragraphs: Organisers to close top tier of Allianz Stadium on Friday

The opening night of the inaugural Nations Championship finals weekend on Friday is poised to be played in front of around 40,000 empty seats, with the top tier of the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham to be closed.

The Guardian has learned that more than 50% of tickets at the 82,000-capacity venue for the Ireland v Australia/Italy v Fiji double-header remained available on Monday. That figure could grow after tournament organisers opened a ticket swap exchange for fans wanting to watch their team.

Ticket sales for Saturday and Sunday are stronger, at 70% of capacity, with Nations Championship officials hoping to sell out Saturday’s England v New Zealand/Wales v Japan double-header and Sunday, when France and South Africa will contest the final after Scotland play Argentina.
Supporters had to wait for the final round of group games to be completed on Saturday to learn which of the six fixture slots each country would play in.
Selling out three successive rugby events was always likely to be challenging, particularly the Friday, with Fiji v Italy kicking off the opening match at 4.40pm GMT.
Tickets have been competitively priced, starting at £60 (£20 for juniors) for Friday, rising to £100 on Saturday (£50 for juniors) and £125 for Sunday (£50 for juniors).

Despite the difficulties of selling tickets at the last minute the Nations Championship is committed to the finals weekend concept, although Qatar have pulled out of hosting in 2028 due to the Middle East conflict, as the Guardian revealed earlier this month.

articles.title: Infantino’s $20bn World Cup sell-off plan was to run for up to 96 years, documents show
paragraphs: Gianni Infantino’s failed Fifa Forward Enterprise plan could have locked football in for up to 96 years while paying its management up to 5% of the scheme’s multibillion-pound value, according to documents seen by the Guardian.

Previously undisclosed communications by Fifa and Thrive Capital, the lead investor for the proposal, cast fresh light on the deal to sell off football’s crown jewels. They outline a plan, produced days before July’s final of the 2026 World Cup, to profit from the sport’s burgeoning commercial revenues for almost a century.
Infantino hopes to be re-elected for a fourth term as president in March and is the favourite to win that contest.
In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.
If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.
If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

An internal Fifa risk assessment dated 17 July, designed as one of the final steps before concluding the FFE agreement, spells out the scheme’s extraordinary scope. “This deal provides for Fifa to create a for-profit subsidiary which would have all the commercial rights for Fifa events transferred to it for commercial exploitation for the next 96 years,” one section reads.

Another internal Fifa document written the following day, outlining the proposed agreement with Thrive, says the deal’s contract period “would be for rolling 12-year licence periods to a sum maximum total of 96 years” and goes further in stating Fifa would assume 51% ownership “in perpetuity”.

articles.title: David Raya’s shoulder injury ‘not too serious’ and no surgery needed for Arsenal goalkeeper
paragraphs: No 1 to miss Dortmund game but could return for City clash
‘We were worried … he’s better than expected,’ says manager
